A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work, with matching authors, core mechanism, and earlier experiments. All 13 pages of v1 and 31 pages of v2 are readable, including equations and figures. Neither contains a standalone appendix; v2's reference to Appendix I concerns a cited paper.

before.justification: Section VI.D and Figures 1–3 report original triangle-counting experiments on the Wikipedia network, averaged over ten simulation runs.

after.justification: Section 7 reports original triangle-counting, runtime, synthetic-graph, and 4-cycle-counting results across multiple networks.

M1.justification: The core hashing, subsampling, and randomized-response framework remains. V2 corrects the written debiasing coefficients, changes the CSS correction from addition to subtraction, fixes triangle-edge indexing, and specifies a two-edge-product counting adaptation for 4-cycles. Clipping was already evaluated in v1; its expanded documentation does not establish a newly introduced component.

E1.justification: V1 evaluates triangle counting on Wikipedia alone. V2 retains this coverage and adds Facebook, Google+, and synthetic power-law graphs, plus the distinct task of 4-cycle counting on the Congress Twitter and email-Eu-core networks.

E2.justification: ARR and ARROne remain the external comparators, including the same sensitivity adjustment. V2 Figure 5 adds GroupRR with CSS and clipping to graph-size and privacy-budget comparisons that included only the smooth-sensitivity variant and ARROne in v1 Figures 2–3. Newly discussed hashing and compression methods are not evaluated as baselines.

E3.justification: V2 adds runtime measurement, root-sum-squared 4-cycle error across ten trials, and a power-law testing protocol with s=5 and epsilon=1. Its upload-study description also changes from explicitly excluding CSS and the four-cycle trick to specifying s=10, CSS probability 0.1, and ARROne probability approximately 0.0316. Figure 3 retains the earlier variant labels, so this establishes a documentation change without establishing how that experiment was executed.

E4.justification: V2 adds a stress test violating the existing degree-bound assumption on power-law graphs (Figure 7), runtime comparisons exposing the speed–accuracy tradeoff (Figure 6), and clipping-versus-smooth-sensitivity comparisons across graph sizes and privacy budgets (Figure 5). V1 lacks the assumption-violation and runtime analyses.

E5.justification: Both versions report averages over ten simulation runs and display shaded bands. V2 introduces no new seed-reporting practice, defined confidence intervals, significance tests, or increased repeated-run count. Its ten-trial 4-cycle error formula concerns the evaluation metric.

E6.justification: V2 adds results for the new networks and task, clipping curves in retained parameter sweeps, runtime measurements, and power-law findings. Section 7.2 reports roughly 1000-fold lower 4-cycle error than ARR at sampling factor 100; Figure 6 shows substantially slower smooth-sensitivity execution than clipping. These are additional findings, not demonstrated same-setting performance improvements over v1.

T1.justification: V2 reformulates privacy through sequences of budgeted queries, expands the amplification argument, and corrects the debiasing derivation. It adds the smooth-sensitivity variance bound in Theorem 12 and clipping guarantees with supporting lemmas in Theorem 13. Theorem 7 now bounds variance before final noise, replacing v1's analysis including Laplace noise under a public-degree assumption.

C1.justification: V2 adds an explicit claim to the first purely local differentially private graph-statistics mechanism leveraging subsampling amplification. Its abstract and conclusion extend the demonstrated performance contribution from triangle counting to 4-cycle counting, including a claimed 1000-fold error reduction. The earlier triangle-counting claim remains.

C2.justification: V2 adds practical justification and applicability discussion for the existing degree-bound assumption, explains why public hashing parameters do not disclose privately selected representatives, and interprets runtime results as a reason to prefer clipping on larger networks. It also removes v1's detailed explanation of the upload-error plateau.

D1.justification: V2 supplies Algorithms 1–4, documents the clipping thresholds explicitly omitted from v1, discloses the clipping failure parameter of 0.001, and expands sampling-parameter guidance and experimental specifications. These substantially improve the available implementation description. The code repository information is retained.

R1.justification: A new related-work subsection contrasts the method with binary/optimal local hashing and universal exact compression, distinguishing their tabular privacy settings from edge-local privacy. V2 also expands coverage of recent butterfly, walk, cycle, and graphlet counting research and strengthens its subsampling-amplification novelty positioning.

P1.justification: V2 reorganizes the four-step presentation into three stages, moves estimator derivations into the theoretical analysis, separates experiments into their own section, and adds dedicated related-work discussion. Method explanations and proofs are extensively rewritten, alongside the terminology change from GRR to GroupRR.

P2.justification: The document changes from two-column to single-column layout and adds mechanism and communication diagrams plus boxed algorithms. Experimental displays expand from three to eight figures; earlier graph-size and privacy plots are combined and extended into Figure 5, while new network, runtime, robustness, and 4-cycle panels are introduced.

improvement.justification: Corrected estimator formulas, previously omitted clipping instructions, and validation beyond one network and triangle counting resolve important weaknesses in v1. Runtime and degree-assumption stress tests substantially improve the evidence about practical applicability. V2 still contains material inconsistencies: its upload settings conflict with Figure 3, and Theorem 13's proof contradicts its stated probability guarantee. These weaken parts of the revision, but the gains in empirical support and inspectable technical detail remain substantial.
